name: lambda-architecture
context: Large-scale data processing systems requiring both batch (historical) and real-time (low-latency) analytical capabilities. Designed to balance data accuracy, throughput, and fault-tolerance for massive datasets by combining batch processing for comprehensive views with stream processing for real-time views.
benefits: Accuracy + Latency: Batch layer ensures accuracy, speed layer provides low latency
Fault Tolerance: Speed layer bugs corrected by next batch run
Human Fault-Tolerance: Can fix bugs by recomputing from raw data
Flexibility: Different technologies for batch and stream processing
Eventual Consistency: System always converges to correct answer
Immutable Data Store: Eliminates update/delete corruption vectors
tradeoffs: Dual Codebase: Batch and speed layers often require different code/implementations
Merge Complexity: Serving layer must correctly merge batch and real-time views
Operational Complexity: Maintaining two processing pipelines doubles monitoring overhead
Consistency Divergence: Results may differ between batch and speed views during reconciliation
High Total Cost of Ownership: Two systems mean double infrastructure, double maintenance
Testing Complexity: Must test both paths and their merge logic
use_cases: Financial reporting dashboards displaying live transaction feeds alongside daily/weekly reports
IoT monitoring systems requiring real-time alerts and historical trend analysis
E-commerce analytics combining real-time inventory with historical sales trends
Security information and event management (SIEM) with real-time threat detection
User behavior analysis needing both session-level real-time metrics and long-term cohorts
Healthcare systems combining real-time patient monitoring with batch reporting
Ad tech platforms needing real-time bid optimization and batch ROI reporting
avoid_when: Simple queries with no real-time requirements
Low data volume where batch-only processing is sufficient
Team lacks expertise in both batch and stream processing paradigms
Strong consistency requirements at all times (batch lag unacceptable)
Data volumes manageable with pure streaming approaches
When sub-second latency is not required for core business functions
Over-engineering for small to medium-scale data processing
component_types: BatchLayer: Master dataset storage and full recompute processing; produces accurate batch views
SpeedLayer: Real-time incremental processing; produces approximate real-time views
ServingLayer: Merges batch and speed views; indexes and answers queries
MasterDataset: Immutable, append-only raw data storage (HDFS/S3)
BatchView: Precomputed query results from full dataset recompute
RealtimeView: Incremental query results from recent data only
MessageQueue: Kafka/Kinesis/Pulsar for durable event ingestion
BatchProcessor: Spark/Hive/MapReduce for scheduled full recompute
StreamProcessor: Flink/Spark Streaming/Kafka Streams for real-time processing
MergeQueryEngine: Combines batch and speed outputs at query time
anti_patterns: Distributed Monolith: Using Lambda but coupling batch and speed layers so tightly they cannot scale independently
Shared Codebase Without Abstraction: Duplicating business logic in both layers without shared libraries causing drift
Neglecting Merge Logic: Underestimating the complexity of the serving layer merge operation
Ignoring Divergence Monitoring: Not implementing reconciliation checks between batch and speed outputs
Insufficient Testing: Only testing individual layers without end-to-end merge verification
Schema-less Core: Storing data without schemas causing merge failures and data quality issues
design_principles: Immutable Master Dataset: Store all historical data in append-only storage; never update or delete
Batch Layer Guarantees Accuracy: The batch layer always produces correct results eventually
Speed Layer Provides Approximation: Real-time views are temporary and will be overwritten by batch
Serving Layer Merges Views: Combine batch and speed outputs for complete query results
Eventual Consistency: Accept transient inconsistencies; system converges over time
Separation of Concerns: Batch and speed layers serve different analytical purposes
best_practices: Shared Transformation Libraries: Build shared UDF libraries used by both batch and speed paths to avoid logic drift
Drift Detection: Implement reconciliation jobs comparing speed output vs latest batch truth continuously
Merge Precedence Rules: Define explicit rules (typically batch wins when views overlap, speed fills gap windows)
Late Data Handling: Explicitly handle events arriving after processing window closes; plan for watermarks
Bounded Speed Views: Keep speed layer state bounded; discard after batch view incorporates that period
Incremental Rollout: Start with one domain, validate through two full batch cycles before expanding
Owner Matrix: Publish clear ownership for ingest, speed, batch, and serving layers
Replay Drills: Run weekly drills to verify late-data and replay capabilities
Cost Validation: Continuously validate cost and replay feasibility as data volume grows
